Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why did my GP give me a different anti-psychotic medication knowing the previous one worked?
Answer: Yes, why did they? There are any number of possible explanations. Maybe your idea of ‘working’ and their idea of ‘working’ differ. Maybe the drug was causing too many harms to be acceptable to the prescriber. Maybe they wanted to try out a different drug to see if it’d be better in some way, like a better ratio of upsides to downsides. Maybe they have enrolled in a trial without you knowing. Maybe they were told to boost their prescribing numbers for this other drug. Maybe there is a temporary shortage or weird pricing going on. Maybe additional interventions conflict more with the previous drug than the new one. Maybe you’re being switched to a different drug source or brand, or being put on a combo drug. Etc. Ultimately, likely the only person to know this GP’s reasoning is them. You have to talk with them to find out what they are doing and why, or at the very least request your medical records with doctors notes intact if they refuse to explain or you can’t talk to them for a long while. It is not typical for a GP to have the expertise to responsibly manage neuroleptics in the first place, but a lot of psychiatrists do a bad job as well so you have to do your own homework either way and assess whether any individual provider is giving you reasonable advice. Also be aware that swapping antipsychotics is probably going to cause withdrawal syndrome and/or other drug symptoms.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the chemical process behind the effectiveness of antidepressants?
Answer: There is no such thing, Mr Spambot. “Effectiveness of antidepressants” is a variably and subjectively defined idea with no particular underlying process. Clinically speaking, “effective” just means causing changes in how someone is thinking, feeling, or behaving that society, the prescriber, or the patient were wanting. There are innumerable ‘hows’ as to the way these changes can be brought about, and the very same changes can be desirable in one patient but adverse reactions in another. The whole idea of “antidepressant efficacy” as a measurable and uniform phenomenon is a marketing myth, not a pharmacological reality. It exists as a concept to facilitate the drug and psychiatric industries but has no scientific basis. We know scientifically that these drugs are doing all sorts of things in the nervous system and the rest of the body which can alter experiences, but none of them constitute “the effectiveness of antidepressants”. Even when we specify parameters for alterations we want to consider effectiveness in a particular situation, the underlying mechanisms involved tend to be incompletely understood, or lacking much outline at all. Since mechanisms are an integral part of marketing messages, drug companies opted to just invent some appealing lies in order to sell drugs better, and that decision is one of the most successful and profitable decisions ever made in the history of mankind.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why is there still so much research being done on depression when for most people taking anti-depressants helped cure it?
Answer: Three reasons: These concerns encompass far more than just patient wellbeing — they impact the costs to society of depression, disability, and adverse drug effects, they shape the way political power is formed and wielded, they respond to class warfare and other economic dynamics within societies, they influence our toxicity to the environment, and so forth. Also note that the majority of research into depression isn’t research into new drug products. The multi-industrial investment in depression research is much more variegated and expansive, and drug companies spend more on marketing current psychiatric drugs and profitable narratives than they spend on developing new psychiatric drugs anyway. So, in short, depression research is a significant convergence of economic and political factors and the everyday citizen has an emotional stake in the wellbeing of others even though those other factors are the real drivers.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are Olanzapine withdrawals life-threatening?
Answer: Olanzapine withdrawals are very commonly severe but not usually outright life-threatening. As with any neuroleptics, olanzapine innately has some fatal risks. These can involve a variety of organ systems and encompass many different mechanisms, when mechanisms are known at all. Reduction-emergent drug effects share this general pool of life-threatening risks, and some will be more common with discontinuation than with general use while others will be less common with discontinuation than ongoing use. Most withdrawal effects are not going to be life-threatening and most patients will not be on the verge of death even if they unwisely cold turkey olanzapine. But, life-threatening risks are usually less of a concern here than serious effects which are not necessarily immediately threatening someone’s life. For example, disability, long-term harm, personal and social losses, and exposure to misdiagnosing and mismanaging are key dangers that are far more commonly experienced. In antipsychotic withdrawal, some of the most common ways in which drug effects may threaten someone’s life include things like heart rhythm problems, akathisia (which is a major suicide risk), neuropsychological crisis (psychosis, mania, etc which may result in dangerous behavior), seizures, and accidents or falls from disorienting drug effects like sleep deprivation, dizziness, blood pressure issues, cognitive impairment.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How does psychiatry address concerns regarding the reliability and validity of psychiatric diagnoses?
Answer: Magic wands. Reliability is measured subjectively and doesn’t too much matter because it doesn’t matter to patients how often doctors select the same diagnosis for the same patient and circumstances. If there is to be any benefit for the patient, the practitioner needs to address the patient rather than the diagnosis. The diagnosis itself is immaterial to the patients in the clinical context, so how popular one selection is compared to the others is meaningless unto itself. Validity is a non-starter. Psychiatry addresses the lack of validity to psychiatric diagnoses by saying psychiatric diagnoses lack validity. Well, in private, or in academic literature, or in blogs and letters that industry marketing will paper over, anyway. Even in diagnostic manuals, if sometimes in roundabout manners. Diagnoses being stated outright as invalid is no obstacle because the marketing and the clinicians will often claim the opposite. Everyone wins, except patients. Magic wands are so valuable to psychiatrists because they help bridge psychiatric claims and reality. Anything is true or correct or helpful if you wave a magic wand which makes it so in your own mind. Reality doesn’t matter except as a jumping-off point for bamboozling people. Psychiatry is not needing to address concerns, it is only needing to wave magic wands. If there were some sort of objective accountability involved, psychiatry would already be dead in the water.
